passage: I'm Shankar, and I practise at the skating rink with Maria, who's nine. Last month she kept falling on the turns and said, "I can't do this," and sat on the side. The coach said something to her I couldn't hear. After that, she started saying "not yet" instead. She fell a lot more, but she got up each time. Yesterday she did the turn without falling. I don't know what she was thinking, but she didn't even cheer; she just did it again.

qa.q: What did Maria say last month when she kept falling?
qa.a: She said, "I can't do this," and sat on the side.

qa.q: What might Maria doing the turn again instead of cheering suggest?
qa.a: It might suggest she was focused on getting better and wanted to prove it wasn't luck.

qa.q: What change helped Maria improve?
qa.a: Saying "not yet" instead of "I can't" and getting up each time she fell.

qa.q: How does Shankar see Maria's change?
qa.a: Shankar notices her new effort but isn't sure what she was thinking inside.

grounding: A friend observes a child shift from "I can't" to "not yet" and improve with effort.

Week one: Elizabeth threw down her pencil. "I can't do long division, Nirmala Aunty. I'm bad at maths."
Nirmala said, "You can't do it yet. Let's do one step at a time."
Week two: Elizabeth did three sums a day, circling each step. She got two wrong but found the mistakes herself.
Week three: In class, the teacher gave a long sum. Elizabeth whispered, "Divide, multiply, subtract, bring down." She got it right and grinned at Nirmala after school.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth throw down in week one?
qa.a: She threw down her pencil.

qa.q: What does Elizabeth whispering the steps in class suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she now believes she can work through it step by step and feels more confident.

qa.q: What helped Elizabeth believe her ability could grow?
qa.a: Nirmala changed "can't" to "can't do it yet" and helped her practise one step at a time.

qa.q: How might Nirmala feel when Elizabeth grins after school?
qa.a: She would likely feel proud and happy that her encouragement worked. 😊

grounding: It shows a child replacing "I can't" with "not yet" and improving through effort over weeks.

passage: "Darshan, you say you're no good at swimming. Let me tell you something. I learned to swim at thirty-five. Thirty-five! In the village pond, all the children laughed at me. I swallowed so much water. I told myself, not good yet. Every morning I went back. First I floated, then I kicked, then one stroke, then two. It took months. Now look, I still swim every Sunday. So when you say you can't, just add 'yet' at the end." Thomas tapped his grandson's shoulder. "And practise."

qa.q: At what age did Thomas learn to swim?
qa.a: He learned to swim at thirty-five.

qa.q: What might Thomas have felt when the children laughed at him?
qa.a: He may have felt embarrassed, but he still chose to keep going.

qa.q: What advice does Thomas give Darshan?
qa.a: He tells him to add "yet" when he says he can't, and to practise.

qa.q: How might Darshan see swimming after hearing this story?
qa.a: He may feel more hopeful, knowing even his grandfather improved slowly with effort.

grounding: An elder tells a story showing ability grows with effort, replacing "can't" with "not yet".

passage:
The bicycle Yogesh borrowed from his cousin was too big, and the only flat road in the colony was muddy after rain. Leela Didi held the back of the seat.

He wobbled, fell into a puddle and shouted, "I can't do it!"

Leela crouched. "You can't do it yet. Yesterday you couldn't even push off."

Yogesh wiped the mud off his knee. He tried again, stood on the pedals, went three metres, and fell.

"Five metres tomorrow," Leela said.

He tried once more before the rain started again. Four metres. "Not yet," he muttered, grinning.

qa.q: How far did Yogesh go on his last try?
qa.a: He went four metres.

qa.q: What does Yogesh muttering "Not yet" while grinning suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he now believes he will get there with practice, and feels hopeful instead of defeated.

qa.q: What did Leela Didi say that changed Yogesh's attitude?
qa.a: She reminded him that he can't do it yet and compared today to yesterday, showing his progress through effort.

qa.q: How might Leela Didi feel when she hears him say "not yet"?
qa.a: She would probably feel pleased that her words helped him keep going.

grounding: Shows a child learning to cycle with a borrowed oversized bike on a muddy road and shifting from 'I can't' to 'not yet'.

passage:
Jaya, nine, threw her pencil down at the kitchen table in their Bhopal flat. "I can't do the eight times table. I'm just bad at maths."

Her father, Vikas, sat beside her. "Last month you couldn't do sevens. Can you now?"

She thought. "Yes... after practising."

"So what's different about eights?"

"Nothing," she admitted. "I just haven't practised."

He wrote "I can't" on a paper and crossed it out. Then he wrote "Not yet."

Jaya picked up the pencil again. By dinner she had eights up to eight times six, and she wrote "not yet" on her own sheet, circled.

qa.q: Which times table did Jaya struggle with?
qa.a: She struggled with the eight times table.

qa.q: What does Jaya circling "not yet" suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: It suggests she now believes she can improve and feels encouraged instead of stuck.

qa.q: What did Vikas do that helped Jaya change her thinking?
qa.a: He reminded her of past progress with the sevens and let her reach the conclusion herself before writing "Not yet."

qa.q: What would change if Vikas had agreed that Jaya was bad at maths?
qa.a: She would probably give up on the eights and believe her ability was fixed.

grounding: Shows a child moving from 'I'm bad at maths' to believing practice will help.

passage:
“I can't do it, Noor-didi. I keep falling.”
Manoj, nine, sat on the lane with a scraped knee, the old bicycle on its side.
Noor crouched down. “Can't? Or not yet?”
“Can't.”
“How far did you go yesterday?”
He thought. “To the gate.”
“And today?”
“To the lamp post.”
“That's further. So your legs are learning. It's not can't. It's not yet.”
Manoj wiped his nose. “Not yet,” he muttered. He picked up the bicycle.
“Hold the back?”
“Only for a bit,” said Noor, “then I'll let go.”

qa.q: Where did Manoj reach today on the bicycle?
qa.a: He reached the lamp post.

qa.q: How did Manoj feel when he said “I can't do it”?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and discouraged, sitting with a scraped knee.

qa.q: How did Noor help Manoj change his thinking?
qa.a: She showed him he was going further each day and replaced “can't” with “not yet.”

qa.q: How might Noor feel when Manoj picks up the bicycle again?
qa.a: She probably feels pleased and proud that he is willing to keep trying.

grounding: A nine-year-old learns to replace “I can't” with “not yet” while learning to cycle.

passage:
When I started swimming lessons at eleven, I was the only one in the group who couldn't put my face in the water. I'm Amandeep. The little kids were already floating.
After the second class, I told Coach Dolma, “I'm just not a water person.”
She said, “You're not a water person yet.”
That word stuck. Every lesson I did one tiny thing more. Face in for one second. Then three. Then blowing bubbles. Then floating with the board.
It took two months. Last Saturday I swam the width of the pool without the board.
I still remember saying I'm not a water person. It sounds silly now.

qa.q: What did Amandeep swim last Saturday?
qa.a: Amandeep swam the width of the pool without the board.

qa.q: How did Amandeep feel at the start of swimming lessons?
qa.a: Amandeep felt embarrassed and discouraged, being the only one who couldn't put a face in the water.

qa.q: Why did Coach Dolma's word “yet” make a difference?
qa.a: It turned a fixed label into something that could change, so Amandeep kept trying one small step at a time.

qa.q: How might Coach Dolma feel watching Amandeep swim the width of the pool?
qa.a: She likely feels proud and happy that her student's effort paid off.

grounding: An eleven-year-old learns that swimming ability grows with effort and changes “can't” to “not yet.”

passage:
Teacher's note, Class 5 maths. Rehana Siddiqui.
In the first fractions lesson, Pooja (ten) pushed her notebook away and wrote “I can't do fractions” across the top.
I didn't erase it. I wrote one word after it in green: “yet.”
For two weeks, she did five practice sums every day with me at lunch. She got most wrong at first. She groaned. She kept going.
Today she solved a sum on the board, explaining her steps to the class. Afterwards she crossed out “can't” in her notebook herself and wrote “can, slowly.”
Next step: I'll pair her with Ritvik, who is where she was two weeks ago.

qa.q: What did Pooja write across the top of her notebook?
qa.a: She wrote “I can't do fractions.”

qa.q: How did Pooja feel when she crossed out “can't” herself?
qa.a: She felt proud and confident, realising her ability had grown.

qa.q: Why is pairing Pooja with Ritvik a good next step?
qa.a: It lets her share her “not yet” experience and strengthens her own understanding.

qa.q: How might Ritvik feel working with Pooja?
qa.a: He may feel encouraged, seeing someone who struggled like him and improved.

grounding: A teacher records a ten-year-old changing “I can't” to “can” through daily effort.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Today in maths we did long division. I got four wrong out of five. I wanted to cry. I wrote "I CAN'T DO THIS" on the back of my book.
Kavitha saw it. She crossed out "CAN'T" and wrote "can't YET."
"That's cheating," I said.
"No. Last month I couldn't skip rope, remember? Now I can do fifty."
So after school, I did three more sums slowly with Papa. I got two right! I'm still not good at it. But I'm better than this morning.
Not yet. Not yet. Not yet.
Anjali

qa.q: How many sums did Anjali get wrong in maths?
qa.a: Four out of five.

qa.q: What was Anjali feeling when she wrote "I CAN'T DO THIS"?
qa.a: Anjali felt frustrated and discouraged, close to tears after getting so many wrong.

qa.q: What could Anjali try next time she gets stuck?
qa.a: She could remember Kavitha's "not yet" and practise a few more sums slowly, as she did with Papa.

qa.q: How does Kavitha see Anjali's mistake?
qa.a: Kavitha sees it as a starting point, like her own skipping rope, not as proof that Anjali can't learn.

grounding: In her diary, a child replaces "I can't" with "not yet" after a friend's example.

passage:
The road outside the village school was all stones and potholes. Gautam fell off the cycle for the fourth time and threw it down.
"I'll never learn. I'm just bad at it."
Sarita didi brushed the dust off his knee. "When I learnt, I fell every day for two weeks."

passage:
At the pool in Osaka, Aiko clung to the edge. Everyone else in her class could swim a whole length.
"I can't," she told Xin, who was floating nearby.
"You couldn't float last month," said Xin. "Now you can."
Aiko thought about that. It was true. She'd been scared to even put her face in.
"Try just to the black line," Xin said.
Aiko pushed off, kicked hard, and reached the line gasping.
"Not a length," she said.
"Not yet," said Xin.
Aiko laughed and pushed off again.

qa.q: Where did Aiko cling at the start?
qa.a: To the edge of the pool.

qa.q: What was Aiko feeling when she clung to the edge?
qa.a: Aiko felt nervous and left behind, since everyone else could swim a length.

qa.q: Why did Xin's suggestion of the black line help?
qa.a: It gave Aiko a smaller goal she could reach, so she could feel progress instead of failure.

qa.q: How might Xin see Aiko's progress?
qa.a: Xin sees Aiko improving step by step, from not floating to reaching the line.

grounding: A child in Japan learns to see her swimming as "not yet" rather than "can't".

I'm Dhruv, Keerthana's older brother. This Christmas break she decided to learn to skate on the colony's new rink.
Day one, she fell nine times. She said "I'll never learn" and cried. I told her it was normal.
Day three, she fell less, and said, "I can't do turns. Not yet."
Day six, she was going around the rink, wobbly, grinning at every corner.
I don't know exactly what changed in her head. But I heard her tell a smaller kid, "You'll get it. I fell nine times."

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling on day one?

passage:
Leela beta, you say you can't do this long division. Let me tell you about the monsoon I was ten.
All the boys in our village swam in the river. I couldn't. Every day I stood on the bank while they laughed. "Shankar is a stone," they said. I told my mother, "I can't swim. I'll never swim."
My uncle heard me. He said, "Not 'can't.' Say 'not yet.'" He took me to the shallow bend every evening. First, just floating. Then kicking. I swallowed half the river.
By Diwali, I crossed to the big rock. The same boys cheered.
Now, let's look at your sum again. Which step is 'not yet'?

qa.q: What did the boys call Shankar?
qa.a: They said, "Shankar is a stone."

qa.q: What was young Shankar feeling standing on the bank every day?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and discouraged, laughed at and sure he would never swim.

qa.q: What choice inside the story turned things around for Shankar?
qa.a: Accepting his uncle's "not yet" and practising every evening at the shallow bend, starting with just floating, turned it around.

qa.q: How might the uncle have felt when Shankar crossed to the big rock?
qa.a: The uncle would probably have felt proud and glad that his patient evenings helped his nephew believe he could grow.

grounding: Shows an elder passing on the idea that ability grows with effort, replacing "I can't" with "not yet".
